Let <MATH_0001> be a property of algebraic spaces over fields which is invariant
under ground field extensions. Given an algebraic stack <MATH_0002>
and <MATH_0003>, we say the automorphism group of <MATH_0004>
at <MATH_0005> has <MATH_0006> if the equivalent conditions of
Lemma <REF_0001> are satisfied.
For example, we say <TEXTITOPEN_0001>the automorphism group of <MATH_0007>
at <MATH_0008> is finite<TEXTITCLOSE_0001>, if <MATH_0009> is finite whenever
<MATH_0010> is a representative of <MATH_0011>.
Similarly for smooth, proper, etc.
(There is clearly an abuse of language going on here, but we
believe it will not cause confusion or imprecision.)

Let <MATH_0001> be a morphism of algebraic stacks.
Let <MATH_0002> be a point. The following are equivalent
<STRUCT_0001>
<STRUCT_0002> for some morphism <MATH_0003> in the
class of <MATH_0004> setting <MATH_0005> the map
<MATH_0006> of automorphism group algebraic spaces
is an isomorphism, and
<STRUCT_0003> for any morphism <MATH_0007> in the
class of <MATH_0008> setting <MATH_0009> the map
<MATH_0010> of automorphism group algebraic spaces
is an isomorphism.
<STRUCT_0004>

This comes down to the fact that being an isomorphism
is fpqc local on the target, see
Descent on Spaces, Lemma
<REF_0001>.
Namely, suppose that <MATH_0001> is an extension of fields and
denote <MATH_0002> the composition
and set <MATH_0003>.
Then the morphism <MATH_0004> is the base change
of <MATH_0005> by <MATH_0006>.
Hence <MATH_0007> is an isomorphism
if and only if <MATH_0008> is an isomorphism.
Thus we see that the property propagates through the
equivalence class if it holds for one.
